# Research pass 2 — Gym exercise pool and structure

> Generated by Claude's Research tool, 21 September 2026, from a prompt written in the
> "STRAVA x CLAUDE" project. Evidence grades were assigned by the tool, not by independent
> appraisal. Most cited studies were named in the text without links and have not been
> individually checked. See `references.md`.

## TL;DR
- **The two-session weekly coverage grid is broadly sound and worth keeping**, but it tries to touch slightly too many capacities every week; the fix is to demote 2–3 low-dose capacities (foot/ankle, trunk anti-rotation, lateral/rotational) to fortnightly or warm-up "tax" slots and protect a genuine minimum effective dose for the things with the best evidence (heavy compound strength, plyometrics, hip flexion, single-leg work).
- **The biggest evidence-backed wins are already partly in the plan**: heavy compound lifts + plyometrics for running economy and durability (well-supported), hip-flexor and hip-abductor strengthening for the athlete's specific failure points (reasonable-to-well-supported), and a carefully gated plyometric progression given his Achilles history (well-supported process, but he must earn entry).
- **What to change**: cut redundancy (too many split-squat variants, too many carry types), add loaded/eccentric hip flexion and a true adductor exercise (Copenhagen), treat "abs" as programmed anti-rotation, and stop expecting upper-body work to do more than posture/arm-drive/health/enjoyment. Do not let any one capacity dominate — the calf-then-hip-flexor over-focus of previous iterations was the mistake.

## Key Findings

1. **Strength training for runners has strong, consistent evidence, and the athlete's favourite lifts are the right anchors.** Multiple systematic reviews with meta-analysis find heavy-load resistance and plyometric training improve running economy in trained runners. The benefit carries into a fatigued state ("durability"), which matters more for a 24-hour backyard ultra than fresh economy does.
2. **The 2026 race failure (hip flexors) is a real, literature-recognised phenomenon.** Hip-flexor function is central to leg swing and is speed-sensitive; simulation work identifies the iliopsoas as a key limiter. But most hip-flexor training evidence comes from sprinters and untrained people, not ultra-runners, so transfer is a reasonable inference, not proven.
3. **Ultra-distance running fatigues the body differently from a marathon** — the dominant signal is large *central* (neural) fatigue plus plantar-flexor and knee-extensor force loss, not a single muscle. This argues for broad resilience, not narrow calf/hip-flexor obsession.
4. **Plyometrics are high-yield but the failure mode is dose and progression, especially with his Achilles history.** There are concrete entry criteria and a validated hopping progression he should follow.
5. **Lateral/adductor and hip-abductor work has decent injury-relevant evidence; generic "core"/anti-rotation has weak performance evidence but is cheap to include.**
6. **Exercise variation should be systematic, not random** — his love of variety is fine if rotations are anchored blocks every 4–6 weeks, not novelty every session.

## Details

### 1. Exercise selection overall

**Running economy & performance (well-supported).** Balsalobre-Fernández et al. 2016 (*J Strength Cond Res* 30(8):2361–2368), a systematic review with meta-analysis of 5 studies / 93 highly trained runners (VO2max >60 ml/kg/min), found a large beneficial effect on running economy and concluded that "a strength training program including low to high intensity resistance exercises and plyometric exercises performed 2–3 times per week for 8–12 weeks is an appropriate strategy to improve RE in highly trained middle- and long-distance runners." Later, larger reviews (Llanos-Lagos et al. 2024, *Sports Medicine*) found high-load training (≥80% 1RM) gives small-to-moderate economy gains especially at faster speeds and in high-VO2max athletes, while plyometric training improves economy particularly at lower speeds (≤12 km/h) — highly relevant to a backyard ultra run at ~6:00/km. Submaximal-load and isometric strength training were less effective for economy.

**Durability (well-supported and directly relevant).** A 2025 RCT (Zanini et al., *Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise*) in well-trained male runners (10 km ~39:00 — essentially this athlete's level) showed 10 weeks of twice-weekly maximal strength + plyometrics improved running-economy *durability*: economy declined only 2.1% over 90 minutes vs 4.7% before training, and fatigued time-to-exhaustion improved 35% vs an 8% decline in controls. The programme used back squat, single-leg press, seated isometric calf raise (~3×6), plus vertical (pogos, drop jumps) and horizontal (hops, bounding) plyometrics — close to what this athlete should run.

**Bilateral vs unilateral (reasonable inference).** Meta-analyses (Moran et al.; Zhang et al. 2026) find no clear winner for transfer to running-relevant qualities — unilateral training transfers best to unilateral tasks, bilateral to bilateral strength, and both raise maximal strength. Practical implication: keep the bilateral anchors (squat/deadlift) for load and keep single-leg work for specificity and asymmetry — which the plan already does. Don't agonise over the split.

**Free weights vs machines (reasonable inference).** For a runner, free-weight compounds are preferred because they load the trunk and stabilisers and carry the direct running-economy evidence; machines are fine as accessories, particularly at the limited gym.

**Muscles that matter most in running (well-supported biomechanics).** Propulsion in running comes primarily from soleus and gastrocnemius, with gluteus maximus, hamstrings and vasti also contributing; the vasti provide braking/support (perturbation-EMG work, Hamner/Delp lineage). Hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) drive leg swing and become progressively more important as speed rises. This supports a pool that covers calves (soleus especially), posterior chain (glutes/hamstrings), quads and hip flexors — the plan does.

**Ultra-specific fatigue (well-supported, distinctive).** After a 65-km ultra, knee-extensor MVC fell ~30% and was *mostly central* in origin (Millet et al. 2002, *J Appl Physiol*). A 24-h treadmill run produced ~41% knee-extensor and ~30% plantar-flexor MVC loss, again predominantly central (Martin et al. 2010, *J Appl Physiol*). A 110-km mountain ultra (PLoS One 2016) showed the greater the peripheral plantar-flexor fatigue, the greater the shift to a flatter, higher-cadence, shuffling gait. **Interpretation:** in a 24-h backyard ultra the limiter is whole-system fatigue resistance, not one muscle. This is the strongest argument in the review for the athlete's own instinct: build broad resilience, weight the known weak links (hip flexors, feet, calves/Achilles) but don't let them monopolise the plan.

### 2. Hip flexion

**Function (well-supported) and performance link (mostly sprinter/untrained evidence).** The iliopsoas is the strongest hip flexor and the main driver of swing-phase leg drive; EMG shows hip-flexor activation rises sharply with running speed. A predictive simulation (*Annals of Biomedical Engineering*, 2026) concluded running speed is maximised by strengthening the hip flexors and adductors, with step frequency most sensitive to hip-flexor strength. Deane et al. 2005 (*J Strength Cond Res* 19(3):615–621, n=24 untrained) found 8 weeks of resistance-band hip-flexor training improved hip-flexion strength by 12.2% and cut 40-yd dash and shuttle-run times by 3.8% and 9.0% respectively, with no change in controls. **Caveat: these are sprint/untrained data; transfer to preventing hour-19 hip-flexor failure in an ultra is a reasonable inference, not proven.**

**Why his hip flexors failed (reasonable inference).** Over 19 hours the hip flexors both drive swing and eccentrically control the trailing leg; they fatigue with sheer repetition and are almost never trained directly. He has *never* trained hip flexion. That, not a mystery, is the likely story: a large, never-strengthened demand meeting an extreme duration. Building both maximal strength AND strength-endurance of hip flexion is justified.

**How to train it (reasonable inference; EMG-guided).** Loaded, longer-lever and eccentric options load the iliopsoas/rectus femoris hardest — cable/band-resisted hip flexion, weighted marches, hanging leg/knee raises (which also load the trunk) and high-knee step-ups. Program BOTH a heavier strength emphasis (e.g. standing cable hip flexion, 3×8–12) and a strength-endurance emphasis (banded marches, longer sets / timed holds) because the race demand is endurance under fatigue. A-skips double as reactive + hip-flexion drilling.

**Mobility vs strength (reasonable inference).** There is a practitioner tension: chronically stretching an already-lengthening, over-worked hip flexor is lower value than strengthening it through range. Keep some hip-flexor/quad mobility for comfort, but the priority is strength through a full range, not passive stretching.

### 3. Reactive / plyometric progression

**Evidence (well-supported).** Plyometric training improves running economy (typically cited 3–8% in reviews of primary trials), increases tendon stiffness and reduces ground-contact time. Cormie et al. 2011 (*Sports Medicine*) frame plyometrics and heavy resistance as complementary (high-velocity vs high-force ends of the force-velocity curve). For this athlete the value is elastic-energy return and retaining a springy stride deep into fatigue.

**Entry criteria given his Achilles (well-supported process).** Per the Silbernagel pain-monitoring model (Silbernagel et al. 2007, *Am J Sports Med* 35(6):897–906, Level-1 RCT) and JOSPT return-to-sport guidance (Silbernagel & Crossley 2015, *JOSPT* 45(11):876–886): begin the loading progression only when activities of daily living cause pain no higher than 2/10; pain during/after loading may reach ~5/10 on the 0–10 scale but must settle to baseline by the next morning and must not escalate week to week. Given recurrent flares, adopt the more conservative Sancho hopping threshold of ≤3/10 during hopping specifically. He should build seated calf strength toward roughly bodyweight and beyond before single-leg hopping — Sancho's data flagged seated heel-raise strength <1.0× bodyweight as a calf-injury risk marker (the one participant who tore a calf was the only Level-4 case below bodyweight, at 0.95× BW).

**Validated hopping progression (Sancho et al. 2019, *Phys Ther Sport* 40:107–116 — feasibility study, n=15 male recreational runners, best available but NOT an RCT).** Four pain-guided levels, progressing only after two successful sessions at the current level:
- **Level 1 (pain >3/10):** isometric seated single-leg heel raises, up to 3×/day, 5×45 s.
- **Level 2 (pain <3/10, exercises tolerated):** add isotonic calf (standing 2×25; seated 3×8 at 80% 6RM) + hip abduction/extension.
- **Level 3 (pain <3/10 AND 20 double-leg jumps tolerated):** add double-leg jump programme 3×/week (e.g. 3×60 DL jumps, 3×30 stiff-knee, 3×5 forward/back, 3×5 onto a step).
- **Level 4 (pain <3/10 AND 10 single-leg hops tolerated):** progress to single-leg hops 1×/week plus running 2×/week at high cadence (~170 spm), easy pace, ≤10% volume increase/week.
Increase hop *speed* before volume/height. VISA-A improved 24 points at 12 weeks; the three adverse events all came from doing explosive activity against advice.

**Dose (well-supported/heuristic blend).** Start ~40–60 low-amplitude ground contacts per session (pogos, skipping), progressing over weeks toward higher-amplitude bounding/box jumps and finally depth drops / single-leg hops. A commonly cited tendon-adaptation dose is ~100 contacts, ~3×/week, though for a concurrent-trained ultra runner doing 2 gym sessions, 1–2 short plyometric exposures weekly is realistic. Keep 48–72 h from the snappiest plyometric/calf work to hard running; do plyometrics fresh, never after a long run. Tendon adaptation is slow: collagen synthesis peaks ~37–78 h post-loading (hence ≥3 recovery days between heavy tendon sessions), meaningful structural change takes ~8–12 weeks, and loading should continue ≥12 months given high recurrence risk and the finding (Silbernagel et al. 2007, *BJSM*) that stretch-shortening/hopping deficits persist at 1 year even after symptoms resolve.

**Fit with the week (reasonable inference).** Low-level pogos/skipping can sit in warm-ups; higher-intensity reactive work belongs early in a gym session when fresh, spaced from heavy calf loading and quality runs.

### 4. Multi-planar / lateral / rotational / trunk

**Hip abductors (well-supported for one injury, ITBS).** Mucha et al. 2017 (*J Sci Med Sport* 20(4):349–355), an 11-study systematic review, found that of five ITBS studies, "three found weakness in runners with iliotibial band syndrome; two were of strong methodological rigor and both of those found a relationship between weakness and injury." Hip-abductor strengthening reduces pain and improves function in ITBS. Evidence for abductor strength preventing other running injuries (patellofemoral pain, medial tibial stress syndrome) is weaker/mixed. This justifies keeping lateral/abductor work (lateral band walks, lateral squats/lunges, single-leg control) as insurance, especially given his 2024 knee history.

**Adductors / Copenhagen (well-supported in football; transfer to runners is inference).** The Copenhagen adduction exercise reliably increases eccentric hip-adduction strength (large effect sizes across RCTs). Harøy et al. 2019 (*Br J Sports Med* 53(3):150–157), a cluster RCT of 35 teams / 652 semi-pro Norwegian footballers, found "the risk of reporting groin problems was 41% lower in the intervention group (OR 0.59, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.86, p=0.008)." Note a 2025 CAE meta-analysis in *Scand J Med Sci Sports* was **retracted**, so lean on the primary RCTs and EMG work, not that paper. Runners suffer far less groin injury than footballers, so this is preventive insurance and adductor balance rather than a proven runner performance intervention — but the simulation evidence that adductor strength aids running speed adds rationale, and he has never trained it, so it is worth adding.

**Core / anti-rotation (weak performance evidence; reasonable to include cheaply).** Systematic reviews (e.g. Silfies et al. 2015; RunningPhysio's synthesis of Kibler, Fredericson, Leetun, Stanton) find limited evidence that isolated core-stability training improves running performance or prevents injury; free-weight squats/deadlifts already load the trunk heavily and recruit multifidus. Practical stance: his "unstructured abs" should become a small amount of *programmed* anti-rotation/anti-extension (Pallof press, dead bug, suitcase carry, side plank/Copenhagen) rather than random crunches — cheap, plausibly useful for posture under fatigue, but do not over-invest.

### 5. Upper body

**Verdict (reasonable inference / honest downgrade).** Arm swing has a genuine metabolic role — Arellano & Kram 2014 (*J Exp Biol* 217(14):2456–2461) found net metabolic power demand was "3, 9 and 13% greater for the BACK, CHEST and HEAD conditions, respectively (all P<0.05)" relative to normal arm swing. But that shows arm *motion* matters, not that gym *upper-body strength* improves economy; there is no good evidence that upper-body lifting improves distance-running performance. Its real value for this athlete is posture under fatigue, arm-drive endurance over 24 h, balanced all-round athleticism, general health and enjoyment.

**Minimum effective dose (heuristic).** With only two sessions, one horizontal push and one vertical/horizontal pull per week is plenty — e.g. bench or dumbbell press paired with a row/pull-up. Pull volume slightly favoured for posture. Dead hangs are cheap grip/shoulder insurance and also address his deadlift grip limitation. Don't let upper body crowd out lower-body priorities.

### 6. Foot and ankle

**Intrinsic foot training (moderate evidence, some running-specific).** Systematic reviews (PLoS One 2022; *J Athl Train* 2022) show intrinsic-foot-muscle training improves foot function, balance and posture measures; a proof-of-concept RCT (Sao Paulo group) found 8 weeks of foot strengthening increased intrinsic muscle volume and improved vertical running propulsive force. Evidence for direct injury reduction or performance is weaker. Given his very sore feet at hour 19, short-foot/toe work and tibialis raises are a reasonable, low-cost inclusion — but keep expectations modest and treat as durability insurance.

**Balance/proprioception (well-supported for ankle sprains).** Balance training has good evidence for reducing ankle-sprain recurrence. For a road backyard ultra, sprain risk is low, so this is lower priority — fold single-leg/unstable balance into warm-ups rather than dedicating slots.

**Relevance to ultra (reasonable inference).** Foot fatigue and soreness over 24 h are real; foot/ankle capacity plausibly helps but is not a headline driver. Keep it small and frequent (warm-up integrated) rather than a full paired slot every week.

### 7. Structure and variation

**Two-session coverage grid — verdict: sound in principle, over-loaded in practice.** Touching every capacity every week is achievable only by giving several capacities a dose too small to matter. Better: protect a real minimum effective dose for the high-evidence capacities (heavy compound anchor, plyometrics, hip flexion, single-leg strength, calf HSR) every week, and *alternate* the lower-yield capacities (foot/ankle, dedicated trunk, lateral/rotational) fortnightly or push them into warm-ups. This also respects his over-enthusiasm risk.

**Variation (well-supported).** Kassiano et al. 2022 (*J Strength Cond Res* 36(6):1753–1762) systematic review: *systematic* variation can enhance regional hypertrophy and maximise strength, but *excessive/random* variation (too-frequent changes, redundant exercises) may hinder adaptation. So his love of novelty is fine only if rotations are anchored in 4–6 week blocks with a stated emphasis — exactly what the plan proposes. Don't change the anchors; rotate accessories.

**Supersets (well-supported for time efficiency).** A 2025 systematic review with meta-analysis (*Sports Medicine*, 19 studies) found supersets cut session time without compromising volume, muscle activation, perceived recovery, or chronic adaptations in strength, endurance or hypertrophy — though with higher internal load/RPE and muscle damage. Pair non-competing movements (e.g. hip flexion + upper pull; calf + anti-rotation) and keep the heavy anchor as straight sets.

**Block periodisation of emphases (reasonable inference).** Sequencing 4–6 week emphases (foundations → strength → power/reactive → durability) is defensible; maximal strength decays only ~2% over ~3 weeks and power qualities persist for weeks without direct training (block-periodisation "residual effects" literature, Issurin), so rotating emphasis while maintaining a touch of each is unlikely to cause detraining. Align the power/reactive block away from any Achilles-symptomatic period.

### 8. Warm-up and cool-down

**Dynamic/neuromuscular warm-ups (well-supported for injury).** Neuromuscular warm-up programmes (FIFA 11+ type: dynamic mobility, balance, plyometric and strength elements, 10–20 min, 2–3×/week) reduce lower-limb injury and improve sprint/jump/balance. A dynamic warm-up is the right pre-session and pre-run choice.

**Static stretching (honest read).** There is moderate-to-strong evidence that routine static stretching does not reduce overall injury rates, and long-duration static stretch (>60 s per muscle) acutely impairs strength, power and running economy; short-duration (≤60 s) within a fuller warm-up is largely neutral and may slightly lower musculotendinous injury risk in high-intensity activity. **Practical:** he can keep his 5–10 min of stretching, but put it in the cool-down (or keep any pre-session holds short, ≤60 s) rather than as the main pre-run prep, and shouldn't expect it to prevent injury.

## Recommendations

### Revised exercise pool by capacity (keep / swap / add)

**Anchors (KEEP — fixed):**
- **Back squat** — keep. Heavy, 3–5×3–6 at ≥80% 1RM in strength blocks. His single at 100kg (110kg×3 with a trainer) shows headroom; progress load.
- **Deadlift / single-leg hex-bar RDL** — keep. Fix the grip limitation with straps on top sets, plus dead hangs / farmer's carries for grip endurance, so grip stops capping the posterior-chain stimulus.

**Calf / Achilles (KEEP, structured):** heavy slow resistance calf raises, both straight-knee (gastrocnemius) and bent-knee/seated (soleus — the key propulsive, endurance muscle). 3–4×6–12, slow tempo. Continues Pass-1 work; do NOT let it dominate.

**Hip flexion (KEEP + ADD load):** keep hanging knee/leg raise, banded march, high-knee step-up, A-skips. ADD standing cable/band-resisted hip flexion as a loadable strength movement (3×8–12) and a strength-endurance option (weighted/banded march for time). Rotate strength vs endurance emphasis by block. Priority weak link — but cap at one strength + one endurance slot; don't over-rotate.

**Single-leg strength (KEEP, TRIM redundancy):** keep Bulgarian/rear-foot-elevated split squat as the main driver and step-up (functional, hip-flexion overlap). SWAP OUT the near-duplicates — you don't need Bulgarian split squat AND RFE split squat AND walking lunge AND single-leg box squat AND skater squat in rotation at once; pick ~2 per block. Keep single-leg RDL for posterior chain/balance.

**Lateral / rotational (KEEP core items, ADD adductor):** keep lateral lunge/Cossack, lateral band walk, landmine rotation/cable chop. ADD Copenhagen adduction (start short-lever, progress) — best-evidenced adductor exercise and he's never trained adductors. Alternate fortnightly, not every week.

**Reactive / plyometric (KEEP, GATE and sequence):** keep pogos, skipping, box jumps, bounding, lateral bounds, single-leg hops, depth drops — but strictly in that difficulty order and gated by the Achilles criteria (Section 3). Start low (pogos/skipping in warm-ups), earn single-leg hops and depth drops. Depth drops are the LAST progression, not an early-rotation option.

**Trunk / anti-rotation (KEEP, PROGRAM it):** convert "unstructured abs" into programmed Pallof press, dead bug, side plank, suitcase carry, bird dog, ab wheel. Low investment; anti-rotation/anti-extension over crunches.

**Foot and ankle (KEEP, DEMOTE to warm-up):** tibialis raises, short-foot holds, single-leg/unstable balance, heel/toe walks — fold most into warm-ups rather than a weekly paired slot.

**Posterior-chain accessory (KEEP, PRIORITISE Nordic/RDL):** RDL, hip thrust, Nordic curl, back extension, KB swing, good morning. Nordic curls and RDLs are highest-value for hamstring resilience; hip thrust is a good glute-max loader. Rotate ~2 per block.

**Upper push / pull (KEEP, MINIMUM dose):** one push (bench/DB press/overhead) + one pull (pull-up/row/lat pulldown; inverted row and single-arm DB row for the limited gym) per week. Dead hangs stay for grip.

**Carries (KEEP, TRIM to 2):** don't rotate five carry types. Keep farmer's (grip + trunk) and one of suitcase (anti-lateral-flexion) or front-rack/overhead (posture). Optional slot as programmed.

### Staged plan
1. **Now → ~6 weeks (Foundations block, Achilles still settling):** groove hip-flexion strength, calf HSR, single-leg strength, trunk; plyometrics limited to low-level pogos/skipping in warm-ups ONLY if daily-life pain ≤2/10. Build seated calf strength toward ≥1.0–1.3× bodyweight. Keep squat/deadlift heavy.
2. **~6–12 weeks (Strength block):** push heavy compounds and loaded hip flexion; introduce the double-leg jump programme once Sancho Level 3 criteria met (pain <3/10, 20 double-leg jumps tolerated).
3. **~12–18 weeks (Power/reactive block):** progress to single-leg hops / bounding once Level 4 criteria met (10 single-leg hops tolerated); depth drops only after that is solid.
4. **Ongoing durability block into race build:** higher-rep strength-endurance for hip flexion, calves and feet; taper reactive/heavy work before key ultra attempts.

### Thresholds that change the plan
- **Achilles pain >5/10 during loading, not settling by next morning, or rising week-to-week** → drop back a plyometric level and reduce calf load; do not push through.
- **Seated heel-raise <1.0× bodyweight** → do not start single-leg hopping yet.
- **Any recurrence of hip-flexor cramp/failure in long runs** → increase hip-flexion strength-endurance volume, not maximal load.
- **New lateral knee (ITB) niggle** → prioritise hip-abductor work temporarily (evidence-backed), then return to balance.
- **Sub-3 marathon called (12–16 weeks' notice)** → shift emphasis toward heavy strength + plyometrics for economy; trim durability/foot volume.

## Caveats
- **Transfer of evidence:** the strongest running-economy and durability data come from trained but not ultra-distance runners (10 km ~39:00 cohorts — a good match for this athlete's fitness, but marathon-and-shorter in race demand). Hip-flexor and adductor performance evidence is largely from sprinters, untrained people and footballers; applying it to hour-19 ultra failure is a reasonable inference, not a proven intervention.
- **The hip-flexor diagnosis is plausible but not confirmed** — "couldn't lift the leg" at hour 19 is consistent with hip-flexor fatigue, but ultra data show fatigue is dominated by central (neural) mechanisms and whole-limb force loss. Training hip flexors directly is sensible; expecting it to fully "solve" hour 19 is optimistic. Broad fatigue-resistance, pacing and fuelling matter as much.
- **Quality of key sources:** Sancho et al. 2019 is a small (n=15), male-only feasibility study, not an RCT — the best available hopping guidance but not high-level proof. The 2025 Copenhagen meta-analysis was retracted; adductor recommendations rest on primary RCTs/EMG. Core-training performance/injury evidence is weak. Some plyometric economy percentages are practitioner syntheses of primary trials rather than the trials directly.
- **Over-enthusiasm is the main risk:** this plan deliberately caps each capacity so nothing dominates. The failure mode for this athlete is doing all of it, hard, every week. Two focused 45–75 min sessions with protected minimum doses and honest recovery spacing will beat an ambitious everything-every-week grid.
